learningObjective: Explain why optional reranking needs a deadline-valid fallback, why mean service time does not identify a tail, and why generated IDs still require live catalog resolution.
mediumRationale: A shared time ruler makes one declared missed deadline visible, instead of compressing many architectural alternatives into tiny nodes. Separate offline and generated-ID examples preserve the placement and validity distinctions without implying a universal production architecture.

mediumComparison.mermaid: Replaced because the many optional branches shrank the labels and hid the concrete deadline and invalid-ID failures the current article asks readers to reason about.
mediumComparison.svg: Selected for a common-scale 0/50/100 ms ruler, a visibly separate offline path, and an actual missing-ID rejection example at readable narrow-screen scale.
mediumComparison.semanticHtml: Rejected because cards could list what changes and what stays, but would make it harder to follow which LLM work happens before retrieval, offline during item preparation, or only after the candidate set is small.
mediumComparison.interaction: Rejected because changing candidate counts or latency budgets would require invented values and hidden state. The durable lesson is the placement and bounded scope of each intervention, not a simulator.
mediumComparison.paperReuse: Rejected because the reviewed sources answer adjacent architectural questions with source-specific figures. Public access was not treated as permission to copy artwork, layout, examples, or wording; the shipped flow is independently authored.
mediumComparison.noVisual: Rejected because the prose distributes the unchanged backbone, three augmentation points, and a generative frontier across several sections. Readers otherwise have to mentally reconcile those claims into one execution path and may infer that every stage is replaced.

pages.insight: The recommender-systems divider opens the relevant neighborhood but contains no mechanism.
The collaborative-filtering slide supplies the unchanged core: user-item behavior, learned user and item embeddings, approximate nearest-neighbor candidate retrieval, scoring, and ranking.
The neighboring content-based and hybrid slide uses item titles, descriptions, and attributes to complement collaborative signal, but predates and does not identify an LLM-specific content encoder.
The personalized-search divider begins the closest application sequence and confirms that the previous two pages are the complete general-recommender neighborhood.

The slide immediately before the LLM examples separates offline ranking metrics from online engagement and retention outcomes; this supports retaining ordinary evaluation and experimentation rather than delegating launch decisions to an LLM.

The first personalized descriptive-search example prompts an LLM with a natural-language query and compact viewing context to return and explain ten ranked titles. It illustrates intent understanding and small-set reasoning, not catalog-scale retrieval.
The second example repeats the same prompt structure for a different user context, reinforcing contextual reranking and explanation while providing no scalable candidate-generation mechanism.
The adjacent comparison slide shows the same descriptive query against existing search products, but contains no architecture or reusable explanatory figure.

The closest architectural slide proposes reranking recommendation candidates with search relevance, reranking search candidates with personalization, and fusing the streams. It supports bounded late-stage augmentation rather than replacing retrieval.
The computer-vision divider closes the personalized-search sequence, confirming that the deck has no semantic-ID or end-to-end generative recommendation slide.

deckReview.notes: GitHub Copilot CLI agent-5 (GPT-5.6 Sol) text-indexed all 214 physical PDF pages for recommender, recommendation, collaborative filtering, content-based filtering, retrieval, ranking, reranking, language model, LLM, and GPT concepts. Pages 129-132 and 141-146 were read as the complete matching recommender and LLM-personalized-search neighborhoods. Page 145 is the nearest pipeline treatment; the deck contains no visual that maps LLM interventions onto a catalog-scale retrieve-then-rank backbone and no generative-retrieval or semantic-ID mechanism. No deck screenshot, wording, prompt, title example, value, or layout is reused.

sources.title: Recommender Systems with Generative Retrieval

sourceReview.notes: The hardest prose-only mental model is the augmentation boundary. A production request may gain an LLM-based intent representation; item text may be encoded offline into content features; and a small top-N set may receive expensive contextual reranking or explanations. Those additions feed or follow the existing catalog-scale path rather than removing it: approximate retrieval narrows the corpus, a learned ranker combines behavioral and content evidence, and online experiments still decide what ships. Semantic-ID generation is shown only as a separate research branch so it cannot be mistaken for the default serving path.

agentReview.summary: Read the complete article, text-indexed all 214 deck pages and inspected both relevant slide neighborhoods, then checked a primary industrial retrieve-rank paper, official recommendation documentation, primary item-language and LLM-reranking studies, and the primary semantic-ID generative-retrieval paper before selecting an original bounded-augmentation flow.

implementation.accessibility: The SVG has a linked title and complete description, directly labeled times and actions, and explicit hold/reject text. Its vertical viewBox and zero minimum width keep the whole comparison visible without horizontal scrolling. Theme tokens support light, dark, and print; current pixel and label checks are recorded separately.

comprehensionRevision.problem: The crowded flow mixed architectural alternatives, rendered very small labels, and did not expose a concrete missed deadline or failed catalog lookup.
comprehensionRevision.change: Show a declared 100 ms call crossing a 50 ms deadline, the valid fast fallback, workload accounting, separate offline work, and rejection of missing generated ID Z.
comprehensionRevision.readerCheck: Can a reader choose the fallback at 50 ms, reject missing ID Z, and explain why neither the illustrated call nor mean service time establishes p99?
comprehensionRevision.evidenceLimit: Expert illustration revision and source arithmetic, not measured learner performance or observed production latency.
